name: Name Resolution vs Connectivity
brief:
A user reports that the school web server is down. It is not. The address answers perfectly well; the name does not resolve.

This is the single most common false alarm in networking, and the test that separates the two takes about four seconds.
watchFor: If ping by address works and ping by name does not, the network is fine and DNS is not. Do not touch routing.

tasks.text: From PC1, ping www.westcta.local and watch it fail to resolve.
Now ping the server by address, 192.168.20.10, and watch it succeed.
tasks.hint: That one result rules out cabling, addressing, gateways and routing all at once.

tasks.text: Run ipconfig /all on PC1 and read the DNS server it is using.
tasks.hint: It is pointing at 192.168.20.99. Nothing lives there.

tasks.text: Point PC1 at the real DNS server, 192.168.20.10.
Ping www.westcta.local by name and get a reply.

extension: Break it the other way: leave DNS correct and shut the link to SW2. Now name resolution and connectivity both fail. Which command tells you which one broke first?
debrief:
Ping by address, then ping by name. If the first works and the second does not, you have a name problem, and every minute spent in a routing table after that is a minute lost.

DNS is a trust dependency. When it is wrong, everything downstream is wrong and the user never sees why.
